doc.title: Warren Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 17, 2018

chapter: Max Roach, M'Boom and Sun Ra
title: M'Boom: drummers' egos, bandleaders' tolerance and openness
summary: Six or seven drummers each hear the beat differently; Roach accepted criticism, as did Ellington and Gil Evans; living with chance.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I love this comment you made about when you had, it might have been M’Boom that you were talking about or some of the other large ensembles, but you said something about, “Everyone has a different idea of where the beat is at.” And I can imagine that’s got to be a little tricky.

Well that was because see there’s a certain ego about drummers. And they all have to be right when they’re in the position of propelling a band. You know the drummer has to be the most constant figure because everybody else can match that. It’s the most audible sound and everybody can feel that vibration so they can lock in to that. But when you have six or seven drummers who are all, I mean all these guys were great musicians, you know, Max had chosen us from his observations and experience with us. Not every one of us could be right you know. The only thing that got us over the first hump was the fact

that we all had so much respect for Max Roach that we just let him lead everything. But when we started presenting our own music, and you might have to criticize Max Roach for something, then you wonder how that’s going to go. But see he was broad enough where he could accept that you know. Now not all leaders can accept criticism of themselves for whatever they do. So they’re locked in a position where if they’re going over a cliff they’re gone. You know. And if you don’t like it just get off the cliff. I mean just get off of their train. But it varies with different people. Some band leaders you can’t tell them a God damn thing. And their music’s going to stay locked right where it is. There are others like Gil Evans, I’ll put Max in that, Duke Ellington was definitely in that category. He could tolerate any kind of crazy behavior because he knew what he wanted out of those musicians. And I think that’s a very important thing. It’s shaped my attitude as a band leader, that I can be a lot more tolerant when things don’t go exactly the way I prescribe because sometimes those ideas can improve your concept, or give you something that you hadn’t thought of before. So it balances out. But you have to have an open mind.
To accept that, that someone heard something that you hadn’t written or proscribed.

Yes. Especially something that you write and it’s got to be correct and it’s got to be this and that. And it’s so prevalent. I did a lot of classical music. I did a lot of symphonies and contemporary music in particular where everything is just so locked in you know. But if you took the piece of paper away from me, or the musical representation that said play an idea, I could do that. There are some people that are so locked in to that, that when you take it away from them there is silence. What am I supposed to do now? And I think that that’s a detriment to musical artistry.
Yeah. Well unlimited choices can sometimes be scary.

Oh yeah, yeah. I mean it’s something that’s a chance. But getting out of bed every morning is a chance. So I have lived with chance all my life. It’s never been, “Oh I’m going to have a million dollars today” and tad at, tad at, tad at. Every day. But see that’s what keeps life interesting for me.
